- When sentiment is consistently negative (especially > 3 consecutive days), model tends to overcorrect downward; reduce forecast bias by 5–10% below historical mean.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >+5% from prior 7-day high), model often overshoots; cap forecast peak at 1.5x prior high or 10% above recent 14-day average.
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive, model frequently overestimates near-term (1–7 day) moves; apply 3–5% downward adjustment for short-term forecasts.
- Model underestimates true mean reversion in 30-day horizon when sentiment is volatile; add 2–4% upward bias to forecast mean to account for lagged mean reversion.
- When sentiment is positive and price is falling, model often fails to recognize reversal; adjust forecast to align with sentiment’s direction, even if price is trending down.
- For 30-day forecasts, if last 3 sentiment values are negative, reduce forecast mean by 3–5% to reflect bearish sentiment persistence.
- If model forecast is >10% above recent 14-day high and sentiment is neutral, apply downward correction to prevent over-optimism.
- When sentiment is positive but price is falling, model often ignores sentiment; adjust forecast to reflect sentiment’s direction, even if price is trending down.
